name: GiveWell (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: each charity it funds, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: GiveWell researches global health and poverty programmes and directs donors' money to the most cost-effective ones; this model covers a gift for its own operations in 2024 ($20.7M, audited), not the $163M of grants it paid out, which are the funded charities' cost and counted in their own models. Its operations aren't short of money (unrestricted gifts were five times its operating costs, the excess granted out), so a further dollar for them mostly frees another donor's dollar for grants and is worth about a dollar granted; the small rest does operations work, where each dollar moved about eleven dollars it caused in 2024 (a quarter of Open Philanthropy's money, all of it shifted, and 59% of other donors' giving, by its own donor survey with non-respondents counted at half, plus $45M its research influenced), each dollar valued at the charities it went to, read live. At the defaults that comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, because a dollar for GiveWell ends up with GiveWell's grantees; the result moves most with the share freed for grants, the value of a life and the discount rate, and no branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Other funding GiveWell's research influenced in 2024 (US$)
rows.explainer: Funders who told GiveWell they gave to programmes outside its Top Charities because of its research ({{row:influenced_funding}}); not in its funds raised, so no double count. Counted with the survey-response step only, and valued at its recipients in value_destinations.

rows.label: Share of Open Philanthropy's giving through GiveWell that GiveWell caused
rows.explainer: Our judgment. All of it counts as shifted money (moved_value), none as new. Open Philanthropy decides its global-health budget itself and has its own global health and wellbeing grantmakers with a bar like GiveWell's; without GiveWell it would still give most of this money to good global-health programmes, so GiveWell is credited with the part its research steers better than Open Philanthropy would alone, set at the low end of the shared own-effect range (facts/meta.json own_effect_share, 15–45%, from Giving What We Can's donor surveys). Low: Open Philanthropy's own team would find nearly the same grants; high: it relies on GiveWell for the research it would otherwise go without.

rows.label: Share of other donors' giving through GiveWell that GiveWell caused
rows.explainer: The share of these donors' giving that would not have gone to equally good charities without GiveWell (the shared own-effect step, normalization.md 2.8: the organisation's own donor survey; whether it was new or shifted money is the separate new-money share). Its 2015 survey's 84%, with the donors who didn't answer counted at half the respondents' influence: 59% (47% to 84%). Above the shared 30% for fundraisers, as expected: the other effective-giving organisations largely recommend GiveWell's charities, so without it there would be little equally good advice to follow.

Value of a dollar to the charities GiveWell funds (its 2024 split, live), units of value
rows.explainer: Where GiveWell's money went in its 2024 metrics year (its metrics report's tables of funds directed by organisation and programme, facts/meta.json givewell_directed_2024_*), each recipient at GiveWell's figure for it on this site, read live under your values (#givewell:<charity>: its programme models weighted by location, the figure the rankings show; GiveWell's own grant models are these destinations, not counted again). Top Charities 76% of the $397M; 21 other recipients with a model; the 16 grants to 14 organisations without one ($4.9M, 1.2%) are valued at the average of the rest. The $45M its research influenced goes to its recipients (Sightsavers, GiveDirectly, Evidence Action, Pure Earth, Dimagi, Fortify Health; Unlimit Health has no model) with equal weights, none being published.

rows.label: Side effects of GiveWell's work beyond the money counted, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for an evaluator whose research is most of its work: {{row:moved_side_effects}} (−10% to +30%) of the modelled value. For GiveWell, positive: its published research and cost-effectiveness models used by funders and governments who don't report it (only funders who told it count in influenced_funding), and other giving organisations' recommendations built on its research beyond the money they pass through it; negative: the staff time charities spend on its reviews, donors' and funders' attention concentrated on what it can measure, and charities shaping programmes to its criteria.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of a dollar all shifted (given anyway, now to a better use), at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: Money that would have been given or spent anyway counts only for the gain over where it would have gone: a grantmaker's grants, or spending that research or advice changed. Its owners spent it, so the organisation is credited its share of that gain (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
rows.explainer: Other donors' money at the net value of a dollar moved (half new, half shifted); Open Philanthropy's at the gain over where it would have gone only, since it would have given the money anyway; both with the side effects.

rows.label: Share of a further dollar for operations that ends up granted out

source.title: GiveWell, Excess Assets Policy; GiveWell, Unrestricted Fund
source.quote: Once we surpass that level of unrestricted assets, we designate the excess assets for granting
source.note: The policy: GiveWell holds enough unrestricted funding to operate for two years into the future and its Board earmarks the excess for granting at least once a year; the excess is designated from 'our largest unrestricted donation or donations' (Unrestricted Fund page). Unrestricted gifts $111M against $21.4M of operations in its 2024 metrics year (Metrics Report 2024, pp. 8, 12), $199M against $23.0M in 2025; net assets without donor restrictions $189M at the end of 2024 (audited statements, p. 3). Read from the Internet Archive's copy; the site itself shows a bot check.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. GiveWell keeps two years of operating needs in unrestricted funds and designates anything above that for granting. The Unrestricted Fund page says most donors' gifts are spent on operations, because the excess is taken from the largest gifts; but a further gift still raises the excess one for one, so it ends up a dollar granted, worth what GiveWell's grants achieve (granted_dollar_value). The rest, where the operating budget does respond to what donors give, does operations work at the next-dollar share of the past average. 95% (80% to 100%), anchored on unrestricted gifts running five to nine times its operating costs.

rows.label: Value of a dollar GiveWell grants (its 2024 directed split, live), units of value
rows.explainer: The funds GiveWell directed in 2024, each recipient at GiveWell's figure for it, read live, the same weights as value_destinations without the funding other funders chose (influenced_funding): what a dollar GiveWell designates for granting achieves.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar you give
rows.formula: next_dollar_freed_for_grants * granted_dollar_value + (1 - next_dollar_freed_for_grants) * uov_per_dollar * donor_cost_share * marginal_vs_past_average
rows.explainer: A further dollar for GiveWell's operations: the share it frees for grants at the value of a dollar GiveWell grants, the rest at the operations' past average, credited by share of resources and scaled to the next dollar.
